label: Isometry and Similarity in Space
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 96 through 106, lifting the plane theory of isometry into three dimensions. The organizing idea is that every spatial isometry is a product of at most four plane reflections, and the sign of the determinant splits all motions into direct and opposite classes.

label: Isometry as Distance Preservation
notes: We model a spatial motion as an affine rule that sends x to Mx plus a translation, where M is orthogonal. Such a map fixes every pairwise distance, and the determinant of M, equal to plus or minus one, records whether sense is preserved or reversed.

label: Reflections Generate Everything
notes: A single reflection fixes its mirror plane and reverses orientation. The fundamental structural theorem states that every isometry of three-space is a product of at most four plane reflections, so reflections are the atomic generators from which all six motion types are assembled.

label: Products of Two Reflections
notes: Composing two reflections always yields a direct isometry. Intersecting mirrors produce a rotation about their common line through twice the dihedral angle, while parallel mirrors produce a translation perpendicular to them with length twice their separation. These are the two simplest direct motions.

label: Euler's Theorem
notes: Euler's theorem asserts that any direct isometry leaving a point fixed must be a rotation about an axis through that point. Because a product of two reflections in intersecting planes is exactly such a rotation, every point-fixing direct motion reduces to a single turn about one line.

label: The Six Isometry Types
notes: The full classification names three direct motions and three opposite ones. Direct: translation, rotation, and screw displacement. Opposite: reflection, glide reflection, and rotatory reflection. The determinant sign separates the two columns, and fixed-set structure separates rows within each column.

label: The Screw Displacement
notes: A screw displacement, or twist, combines a rotation about an axis with a translation along that same axis. It is the generic direct isometry and has no fixed point. Its orbits are helices of constant radius advancing a fixed axial step after each full turn.

label: Rotatory Reflection
notes: A rotatory reflection rotates about an axis and then reflects in the plane perpendicular to that axis. It is the generic opposite isometry. The special case of a half-turn followed by that reflection gives the central inversion, which reverses sense in three dimensions.

label: Central Inversion
notes: Central inversion sends each point to its antipode through a fixed center, the rule x maps to minus x at the origin. In space it is the product of three perpendicular plane reflections, so its determinant is minus one and it is opposite, unlike the direct plane half-turn.

label: Similarities in Space
notes: A non-isometric similarity has a fixed center and combines a rotation about an axis with a dilatation by a scale lambda. The model rule scales by lambda after rotating, and since the spatial determinant is lambda cubed, a negative scale factor reverses orientation while a positive one preserves it.

label: Recap and Invariants
notes: Read the chapter through invariants: distance preservation defines isometry, determinant sign splits direct from opposite, and the fixed set names the type. Signed tetrahedron volume replaces signed area as the spatial sense detector, and at most four reflections rebuild every motion.
